origin: Derived from a pilot on 30 randomly selected papers (seed 20261114). Limitation statements in the pilot papers were extracted and open-coded with LLM assistance (Claude) into 14 provisional themes; the first and second author consolidated these into 11 fields in three groups.
rules: Own work only. Record limitations the authors state about their own approach, system or evaluation. Ignore statements about prior work, background, baselines or other systems, the authors' prompt texts or examples, and weaknesses of LLMs in general that the authors do not tie to their own approach.

Framing. A statement counts only if the authors present it as a weakness, shortfall, cost, risk, open problem or untested condition of their own work. Do not count: neutral descriptions of the design or setup ('we evaluate on CrossCodeEval', 'the token budget B is fixed'); measurements reported without being presented as a drawback; results presented as an advantage ('the maintenance cost is small'); or speculation about what a stronger model might add. Costs: an extra cost of the approach counts if the authors present it as a cost or overhead of their approach, even if they call it acceptable or reasonable. It does not count if they describe it as small, modest, negligible, imperceptible or amortised, or if they mention it to show that the approach saves cost or time overall.

Where to look. Read the sections on limitations, threats to validity, discussion, conclusion and future work in full. Statements elsewhere in the paper (including results and appendices) count only if they meet rule 2 on their own; cue words such as limitation, drawback, overhead, cannot, does not, not yet, only, fails, future work and beyond the scope help to find them.

Boilerplate. A statement is boilerplate if it would be equally true of any other paper: it names no specific model, benchmark, metric, component, setting or number of this study ('results may not generalise', 'as with any empirical study', 'our work has some limitations'). Boilerplate fills no field. A threat to validity that names a specific aspect of this study counts, even if the authors describe a mitigation, unless they state that the threat was ruled out.
LLM judges. An LLM judge used to evaluate the paper's results belongs to F3 Evaluation quality; an LLM judge or other signal used inside the mechanism belongs to F4 Memory quality.

Future work. A future-work item counts only if it names a specific thing the current work does not do, have or test, and is recorded under the gap it implies ('extend to other programming languages' is F1; 'transfer skills across models' is F5; 'we have not built a reduce operator' is F11). Vague directions ('explore further', 'richer policies', 'a promising extension', 'improve efficiency') do not count.
One field per statement. Record a statement under the single field that best matches what the authors say is limited. Use a second field only if the statement contains two distinct limitations.

Field boundaries. Missing or irrelevant accumulated experience or memory is F5; restriction to some tasks, models, languages or benchmarks is F1. Few tasks, items or problems is F1; too few runs, no seeds, variance or significance testing is F2; a benchmark that measures the wrong thing, is contaminated, capped or saturated is F3. A memory or retrieval design acknowledged as simple is F6; other functionality not yet built is F11. Wrong content that the mechanism stores or acts on is F4; errors in the agent's outputs or actions are F10. Pressure on the context window is F7; tokens, money, time or hardware is F8.
Doubt. If you are unsure whether a statement meets rules 1 to 4, do not count it.
A field is filled if the paper states at least one limitation of that kind; how often it is stated does not matter.
Every filled field needs at least one verbatim quote from the paper, with its page. Quote the sentence that states the limitation, not the surrounding description.

fields.name: Generalizability
fields.definition: The approach was evaluated on few models, languages, tasks, benchmarks, settings or small samples, or is inherently restricted to some tasks or dependent on the underlying model or agent.

includes.description: Only a small number of LLMs, or a single model family, were evaluated.
includes.example: Nothing in the design is model-specific, and every LLM role is bound fromaconfigurationtable,butwehavenotrunacross-family replication and cannot claim one.

includes.description: Evaluation is restricted to one (or few) programming languages.
includes.example: First, MemOp is evaluated across four benchmarks, three programming languages, and eleven SE activity categories (§4.4, §F.1). Extending this evaluation to further programming languages and SE activities is a natural next step.

includes.description: Evidence comes from one task type, domain or benchmark family.
includes.example: Future work will explore extending this framework beyond code generation to broader reasoning tasks and dynamic agentic workflows.

includes.description: The approach was not tested in other agent frameworks, harnesses or deployment settings (e.g. streaming, distribution shift).
includes.example: Future work could extend this framework to strictly streaming task settings

includes.description: Few tasks, items, problems, competitions or corpora were used, including a benchmark with few items.
includes.example: Ten items is few

includes.description: The mechanism suits only some tasks, inputs or failure types.
includes.example: It buys least where they are semantic

includes.description: Benefits depend on the underlying LLM/agent, or are limited to homogeneous models, or may vanish with stronger models.
includes.example: We acknowledge that the case for architectural control flow may diminish as LLM capabilities in- crease.

fields.name: Weak experimental validation
fields.definition: Analyses that would support the claims were not done: ablations, sensitivity, baselines, quantitative evaluation, cost measurement, repeated runs, causal or statistical support.

includes.description: Components, variants or hyperparameters were not isolated or varied.
includes.example: Results suggest stability at λ = 0.5; broader sensitivity remains unquantified.

includes.description: No or limited comparison against baselines or alternative designs.
includes.example: The Leviathan results demonstrate absolute capability but do not include a controlled comparison against a baseline agent without SOMA’s memory architecture.

includes.description: The paper lacks systematic quantitative evaluation.
includes.example: This paper documents architectural decisions and design rationale but lacks systematic quantitative evaluation.

includes.description: The analysis cannot establish causality, uses single runs without seeds, variance or significance testing, or uses optimistic/pooled statistics or post-hoc designed instruments.
includes.example: These proportions describe usage rather than independently establish each source’s causal contribution.

includes.description: End-to-end cost of the mechanism was not evaluated.
includes.example: evaluate the end-to-end cost of skill acquisition, maintenance, and use.

fields.name: Evaluation quality
fields.definition: The metrics, judges, oracles or benchmarks used to evaluate the approach may not measure what is intended.

includes.description: Metrics are proxies or miss quality dimensions.
includes.example: Answer-sufficiency is a proxy for task help, not task completion.

includes.description: The evaluation relies on LLM judges that may be biased or differ from humans.
includes.example: the question-quality evaluation in RQ3 relies on LLM-as-a-judge

includes.description: Correctness of outputs is hard to verify automatically.
includes.example: Secondly, unlike traditional function-level code generation approach, automating the evalua- tion of general-purpose software is exceptionally challenging. Though recent efforts aimed to em- ploy Human Revision Cost (Hong et al., 2024), manual verification is still impractical.

includes.description: Models may have seen benchmark data in training.
includes.example: Our de- contamination procedure relies on structured reason- ing traces to detect memorization, which were not available for the harness-free model outputs.

includes.description: The benchmark is capped or saturated for the setting. (A benchmark with few items is F1 Small evaluation sample.)
includes.example: The current OOLONG suite caps at 1M tokens, a ceiling that the raw Opus 4.6 context window already exceeds. Keeping evaluation meaningful as context lengths grow will require benchmarks that scale with them.

fields.name: Memory quality
fields.definition: The information or signals the mechanism stores or acts on may be wrong: noisy or LLM-judged feedback, missing ground truth, polluted entries.

includes.description: Signals used by the mechanism (success/failure, quality, utility) come from LLM judges or stochastic estimates and may be wrong.
includes.example: This agreement supports consistency with human judgment, but does not establish whether scores predict repair gains on unseen CVEs.

includes.description: The mechanism needs ground-truth labels, anchors or verifiers that may be unavailable.
includes.example: With no anchor the loop optimizes noise

includes.description: Stored knowledge may be contaminated across contexts or by bad entries.
includes.example: A global L3 improves cross-project transfer but may introduce cross- project contamination if not managed carefully.

fields.name: Limited experience
fields.definition: Benefits depend on the availability, order, relevance or reach of accumulated experience or captured knowledge: cold start, no similar past tasks, plateauing gains, bounded by sources, no transfer across projects or models.

includes.description: Effectiveness drops when no similar prior experience exists (novel tasks).
includes.example: issues solved exclusively by DARS highlight a limitation of ExpeRepair: its effectiveness drops when relevant prior experience is unavailable.

includes.description: Early-phase instability, sparse evidence or dependence on task order.
includes.example: As shown in Figure 7, all repositories exhibit high volatility during the early phase.

includes.description: Usefulness is limited by what is captured in documentation, history or interactions.
includes.example: The binding constraint is capture.

includes.description: Gains from accumulated memory plateau.
includes.example: Django’s cumulative resolution rate stabi- lizes around issue 80 at approximately 60%, which may be attributable to diminishing returns from repeated memory and the increasing heterogeneity of the remaining issues.

includes.description: Knowledge is not transferred across projects, models or deployments.
includes.example: The ACE playbook currently operates per-project with effectiveness scoring and semantic retrieval.

fields.name: Memory representation
fields.definition: The memory or knowledge design is acknowledged as simple: similarity-only retrieval, flat or minimal representation, static knowledge.

includes.description: Retrieval is similarity/embedding based only.
includes.example: We intentionally adopt simple embedding- based retrieval and straightforward consolidation to better isolate the effect of content quality.

includes.description: Memory is flat, non-compositional, minimal, or modelled in a simplified way.
includes.example: Our current system design is intentionally minimal

includes.description: Knowledge is injected once and not refreshed during execution.
includes.example: However, dynamic acquisition would inevitably introduce additional cost; explor- ing how to balance knowledge freshness and computational cost remains an open challenge.

fields.name: Context limitation
fields.definition: Problems caused by the finite context window: budget pressure, instruction decay, loss through compression or summarisation.

includes.description: Content competes for a finite context window; token accounting is unreliable.
includes.example: Loading all MCP tool schemas at startup consumed 40% of the context budget before the agent processed its first user message.

includes.description: Instructions lose influence as conversations grow.
includes.example: 3.2 Steering Behavior Over Long Horizons System prompt influence decays as conversations grow. Instructions that reliably govern the agent’s first few turns are routinely violated after 30 or more tool calls, when the instruction is far from the model’s attention window and buried under dozens of tool results.

includes.description: Summarising/compressing context loses or distorts information.
includes.example: A subtlety: iteratively summarizing a summary accumulates distortion over multiple rounds.

fields.name: Resource overhead
fields.definition: The approach costs extra tokens, money, training compute, latency, memory or special hardware.

includes.description: The approach consumes more tokens/API cost.
includes.example: The native Bayesian rows spend more tokens

includes.description: Training requires more compute/time/memory.
includes.example: Training overhead. The K-step unrolling training pipeline requires K+1 sequential forward passes through the backbone per training iteration (one warmup pass plus K unrolled steps), compared to a single for- ward pass in standard dLLM training. This multiplicative increase in computation directly raises wall-clock training time and GPU memory consumption, as intermediate activations must be retained across steps for backpropagation through the unrolled computation graph, although the recurrent modules themselves are lightweight (∼0.6% of backbone parame- ters).

includes.description: Inference adds latency or memory.
includes.example: In this study, sam- pling functions and class methods based on rel- evance required the use of a text embedding model. When the number of code files in the repository is excessive, this may reduce the sampling rate, leading to increased completion latency.

includes.description: Requires special hardware (e.g. local GPU).
includes.example: The SGLang integration requires a GPU with sufficient VRAM (24GB+) and is not applicable to API-only deployments.

fields.name: Manual configuration
fields.definition: Templates, prompts, thresholds or hyperparameters are hand-crafted or hand-tuned and may need recalibration.

includes.description: Templates, categories or prompts were designed manually and may lack coverage.
includes.example: The 24-template reminder catalog and its injection timing were manually engineered based on observed failure modes.

includes.description: Thresholds/hyperparameters are fixed or empirically tuned and may need recalibration.
includes.example: Current parameters - the 70% compaction threshold, 3 nudge attempts, 6 thinking depth levels - are globally fixed.

fields.name: Agent reliability and safety
fields.definition: The agent produces imperfect artefacts or actions, or running it poses safety or security risks.

includes.description: Generated code or systems are simplistic or contain residual errors.
includes.example: The chess engine has a known 13-node error at depth 5, consistent with an en-passant-discovers-check edge case.

includes.description: Agents take imprecise or suboptimal actions (edits, tool choice).
includes.example: Agents default to text search (grep) for nearly every lookup, even when a more precise tool exists. This wastes iterations and floods the context with false positives.

includes.description: Generated code runs without isolation, posing security risks.
includes.example: While challenges such as execution security remain

fields.name: Incomplete implementation
fields.definition: Functionality the authors consider needed is not yet supported, including integration with model training.

includes.description: Functionality the authors consider needed is not supported yet.
includes.example: First, we plan to extend OpenSage to support AI-generated workflows.

includes.description: The approach is not integrated with model training (distillation, RL) or has a training-inference gap.
includes.example: help close the training-to-inference extrapolation gap

changes: 1.1 (2026-11-16): rules clarified after a calibration run of both LLMs on the 30 pilot papers, before any non-pilot paper was extracted and before the human evaluation. Added rules on framing (including when a cost counts), where to look, boilerplate, future work, one field per statement, field boundaries and doubt. Sharpened two include items (F2 repeated runs, F3 benchmark ceiling). No field was added, removed or renamed. Version 1.0 is kept in archive_v1.0/.
